Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the primary and secondary stabilizers of the elbow.
Discuss indications for the surgical and nonsurgical management of elbow dislocations.
Describe treatment options for elbow dislocations.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Elbow dislocations are classified as simple (no fractures) or complex (with fracture). The elbow
joint has primary and secondary stabilizers (Figure 1).

Figure 2 Diagram shows how the static constraints of the elbow are analogous to the
defenses of a fortress. The primary static constraints to elbow instability are the ulnohumeral
articulation, the anterior bundle of the medial collateral ligament (MCL), and the lateral
collateral ligament (LCL) complex, including the lateral ulnar collateral ligament. The
secondary constraints include the capsule, the radiocapitellar articulation, and the common
flexor and extensor tendon origins. (Adapted with permission from the Mayo Foundation for
Medical Education and Research, Rochester, MN.)
Secondary stabilizers: radiocapitellar articulation, elbow capsule, surrounding musculature
Terrible triad injuries are complex elbow injuries that include a torn lateral collateral ligament
(LCL), a radial head and/or neck fracture, a coronoid process fracture, and a medial collateral
ligament (MCL) injury. These injuries are called terrible because, without proper management,
they are associated with poor clinical outcomes, including persistent instability, stiffness, and
posttraumatic arthritis (Figure 3).

Figure 3 Images of the right elbow of a 38-year-old woman. AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs
demonstrate a terrible triad injury. C, Intraoperative photograph obtained through the Kocher
interval shows the comminuted, unrepairable radial head fracture. Because the fracture was
deemed unrepairable, arthroplasty was selected for management. D, Intraoperative
photograph shows a radial neck cut. After the radial head was excised, visualization of the type
II coronoid fracture improved. Postoperative AP (E) and lateral (F) radiographs demonstrate
open reduction and internal fixation of the coronoid fracture with the use of two 3.0-mm
cannulated screws and a metallic, modular radial head arthroplasty implant. (Reproduced
from Mathew PK, Athwal GS, King GJ: Terrible triad injury of the elbow: Current concepts. J Am
Acad Orthop Surg 2009;17[3]:137-151.)
Most simple elbow dislocations can be managed nonsurgically; however, terrible triad
injuries are almost always managed surgically to restore elbow stability. Surgical fixation
includes coronoid fracture fixation (and/or anterior capsulodesis), radial head/neck fixation
or replacement, LCL reconstruction, and possible MCL reconstruction.

Epidemiology

Epidemiology
Elbow dislocations are the second most common joint dislocation in adults and the most
common joint dislocation in children.1 Most elbow dislocations are posterolateral. Most
elbow dislocations can be managed nonsurgically; however, terrible triad injuries are
almost always managed surgically.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
Key bony structures (Figure 4)
Figure 4 Photographs of a cadaver model elbow. Anterior (A) and posterior (B) views in the
coronal plane and view in the sagittal plane (C) show distal humeral articular angulation. D,
View in the sagittal plane shows proximal ulnar articular angulation. (Reproduced from Morrey

ME: Anatomy, biomechanics, physical examination, and imaging of the elbow, in Parvizi J, ed:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update, ed 13. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2021, pp 321-339.)
Coronoid process: an important anterior and varus stabilizer of the ulnohumeral joint
Anatomic components of the coronoid process include the tip, body, anterolateral facet,
and anteromedial facet. The O’Driscoll fracture classification is based on the fracture
location of these regions.2
Traditionally, the coronoid was classified solely based on the amount of bone that the
fracture knocked off. Type 1 injuries were the tip of the coronoid, type 2 injuries included as
much as 50% of the coronoid, and type 3 injuries were greater than 50% of the coronoid;
however, this classification system did not consider the importance of the anteromedial
facet of the coronoid. The anteromedial facet is the attachment point of the anterior
bundle of the MCL and, therefore, is an important stabilizer of the elbow.
The coronoid fragment usually has some anterior capsule attached, which can be useful for
soft-tissue repair of the fracture. Even if the coronoid fracture cannot be repaired, the
anterior capsule usually can be tied back down to the coronoid, aiding in restoration of
elbow stability.
Radial head/neck
The radial head/neck is an important secondary valgus stabilizer. It provides approximately
30% of valgus stability with intact medial ligaments. It is the primary stabilizer if the MCL is
torn.
The radial head is a primary restraint to posterolateral rotatory instability.
Restoration of the radial column with repair or replacement, is required to restore elbow
stability in patients with a terrible triad injury.
In general, simple fractures of the radial head can be fixed; however, if more than three
fragments are present, replacement may be a better option.3

Osteology
The osteology of the elbow joint includes the ulnohumeral articulation and the
radiocapitellar articulation. The distal humerus has lateral and medial columns. The
lateral column ends in the capitate, a rounded end to the bone that articulates with the

9/4/26, 9:47 AM
AAOS | Terrible Triad of Injuries of the Elbow
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004092
6/25

radial head. The medial column joins with the lateral column to form the trochlea, a
tongue and groove joint that articulates with the proximal ulna (Figure 1).
Vascular Anatomy
The brachial artery splits into the radial and ulnar arteries at the elbow joint. This area may be
injured, particularly in children; however, vascular injury that requires repair is rare after an
elbow dislocation.
Neural Anatomy
Three main nerves traverse the elbow joint: the median, ulnar, and radial nerves. Nerve
injuries can occur; however, they usually are stretch neuropraxic injuries that improve with
nonsurgical, expectant management (Figures 5 and 6).
Figure 5 Illustration of the anatomy of the antebrachial fossa shows potential sites of
compression of the median nerve, radial nerve, and posterior interosseous nerve (PIN). AIN =
anterior interosseous nerve, ECRB = extensor carpi radialis brevis, ECRL = extensor carpi

radialis longus, FDS = flexor digitorum superficialis. (Courtesy of Michael Lin, MD, PhD, Orange,
CA.)
Figure 6 Illustration of the anatomy of the cubital tunnel shows potential sites of ulnar nerve
compression. FCU = flexor carpi ulnaris, FDP = flexor digitorum profundus. (Courtesy of
Michael Lin, MD, PhD, Orange, CA.)
The median nerve is located just medial to the biceps tendon. It passes from the medial
aspect of the arm to traverse between the superficial and deep flexor muscles of the
forearm.
The ulnar nerve is located medially, in the cubital tunnel. A posterolateral dislocation or long-
term instability may lead to tardy ulnar nerve palsy from valgus instability at the elbow.
The radial nerve traverses the elbow joint just lateral to the biceps tendon. It can be most
easily found in the brachialis-brachioradialis interval just proximal to the elbow and then
travels through the supinator to the posterior forearm.

Tendons
The flexor pronator mass originates off of the medial epicondyle.
The common extensor tendon originates off of the lateral epicondyle.
These muscle masses and their associated tendons act as secondary stabilizers of the elbow
joint.
Joints and Ligaments
Lateral ligamentous complex (Figure 7)
Figure 7 Photographs of a cadaver model elbow. A, The medial ulnar collateral ligaments are
areas of capsular thickening that provide stability to the medial side of the elbow joint. The red
dashed line is the anterior band of the anterior bundle. The black dotted line is the posterior
band of the anterior bundle. The blue dotted line is the posterior bundle. The yellow dotted
line is the transverse bundle. B, the lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL) complex is shown.
The lines represent the approximate orientations of the radial collateral ligament (RCL) and the
LUCL on the lateral side of the elbow. The yellow outline is the location of the annular ligament
attachment proximal and deep to the ligamentous complex but intimately associated with it.
The blue outline represents the ligamentous attachment site on the ulna of the LUCL proper.
(Reproduced from Morrey ME: Anatomy, biomechanics, physical examination, and imaging of
the elbow, in Parvizi J, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update, ed 13. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 321-339.)

The LCL is always injured in patients with a terrible triad injury and usually is avulsed off the
lateral epicondyle with a portion of the extensor muscles.
The LCL complex is the primary restraint to posterolateral rotatory instability of the elbow; it
prevents external rotation of the radius and ulna relative to the humerus.
The LCL is a confluence of three subligaments, including the lateral ulnar collateral ligament,
the radial collateral ligament, and the annular ligament.
MCL (Figure 8)
The anterior bundle of the MCL is the most important stabilizer of valgus stress to the elbow.
If the MCL is injured, the radial head becomes an important secondary stabilizer to valgus
instability.
In patients with a terrible triad injury, excellent outcomes can be attained without MCL repair
if all articular fractures and the LCL are repaired or reconstructed and the elbow joint is
stable. MCL repair may be performed in patients in whom stability is not achieved after LCL,
coronoid, and radial head reconstruction.
Figure 8 Illustrations of the elbow show the structure of the medial collateral ligament
complex (A) and the lateral collateral ligament complex (B). (Reproduced from Tashjian RZ,
Katarincic JA: Complex elbow instability. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006;14[5]:278-286.)
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
A terrible triad injury usually results from an axial load to the elbow during a fall or from blunt
force trauma. The injury begins with disruption of the LCL, followed by failure of the anterior
capsule and the MCL, with fractures of the radial head and the coronoid.
Two main fracture patterns result in instability of the elbow: terrible triad injuries and
anteromedial facet injuries of the coronoid (Figure 2). Both patterns should be assessed for if
an elbow dislocates, especially if the elbow is unstable after reduction (Figure 9).

a bicycle crash show an anterior medial coronoid process fracture. A, AP radiograph
demonstrates an O’Driscoll type 3 anteromedial coronoid fracture. B, Lateral fluoroscopic
image shows tendency toward marked instability of the elbow as evidenced by the ease with
which the elbow dislocated, even with gentle passive extension. AP (C) and lateral (D)

2016, pp 295-308.)
Risk Factors
Most terrible triad injuries result from falls or blunt force trauma.
Associated Injuries
Terrible triad injuries often occur in patients who sustain blunt force trauma.
In addition to management of the elbow injury, a thorough secondary examination is
performed to assess for concomitant upper extremity injury.
Injury Classification
A terrible triad injury is, by definition, a combination of three individual injuries. Injury
classification systems are available for radial head fractures and coronoid fractures.
Radial head fractures are categorized according to the Mason classification system, which
combines radiographic fracture characteristics with clinical findings of joint motion4 (Figure
10).
Type 1: less than 2-mm of displacement; no block to motion.

Type 3: comminuted fracture; block to motion.
Type 4: fracture with associated elbow dislocation

Coronoid fractures are categorized according to the Morrey or O’Driscoll classification
systems. The Morrey classification system focuses solely on the amount of the coronoid that
is fractured(Figure 11), whereas the O’Driscoll classification system includes a subset for
anteromedial facet fractures (Figure 12). In general, involvement of greater than 30% of the
coronoid, or an anteromedial facet fracture, increase the likelihood of instability.
Figure 11 Drawing of the elbow shows the locations of coronoid process fractures according
to the Regan and Morrey classification of coronoid process fractures. Type I fractures consist
of the tip of the coronoid process. These fractures result from a shearing injury to the
coronoid rather than avulsion injuries. Type III fractures and, to a lesser extent, type II
fractures are associated with elbow dislocation and instability. (Reproduced with permission
from Regan W, Morrey BF: Fractures of the coronoid process of the ulna. J Bone Joint Surg Am
1989;71[9]:1348-1354.)

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Typically, the patient history includes a fall on an outstretched arm.
A dislocation also can result from high-energy and low-energy injuries.
Physical Examination
Stability of the elbow should be assessed. Posterolateral rotatory instability should be
assessed via the pivot shift test. The lateral pivot shift test assesses lateral elbow stability
(Figure 13). The test is performed with the patient in the supine position. The arm is held over
the patient’s head, and the arm is moved from an extended to flexed position. While flexing
the arm, the forearm is supinated, and axial compression is applied with a valgus load. A
positive test is noted if subluxation of the radiocapitellar joint occurs.5

Figure 13 Illustration shows the lateral pivot shift test for posterolateral rotatory instability of
the elbow, which is performed with the patient’s arm overhead. A supination-valgus moment is
applied during flexion, causing the elbow to subluxate maximally at approximately 40° of
flexion. Additional flexion causes reduction (with a palpable, visible clunk, if successful). This
test creates apprehension in the patient, who notes the sensation that the elbow is about to
dislocate. (Reproduced from Browdy J, Hauck G: Dislocations and fracture-dislocations of the
elbow, in Limpisvasti O, ed: The Sports Medicine Field Manual. Rosemont, IL, American Academy
of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2015, pp 265-272.)
If posterolateral rotatory instability is present, a dimpling of the skin overlying the dislocated
radial head often is observed. Although a subtle physical examination finding, this may be
indicative of instability if present.
Assess for ecchymosis on the medial side, which may represent an MCL injury or anteromedial
facet fracture of the coronoid.
Examination of the stability of the wrist also is important. Instability at the wrist may result
from an Essex-Lopresti lesion, which is a longitudinal disruption of the interosseous
membrane (Figure 14).

Neurovascular Examination
A complete neurovascular examination should be performed to ensure proper function of the
radial, ulnar, and median nerves. Sensory and motor function can be assessed at the hand.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Pre-reduction and post-reduction AP and lateral radiographs of the elbow should be obtained
(Figure 2). Radiographs should be examined for anteromedial facet fractures of the coronoid
and capitellar fractures, which may be missed (Figure 9).
If wrist instability is questionable, PA and lateral wrist and forearm radiographs may help
identify interosseous membrane instability.
Radiographs of the entire humerus and forearm should always be obtained to asses for other
injuries of the extremity.

complex three-dimensional structures (Figure 15).
Two- and three-dimensional CT reconstruction images may be very helpful.

The arrow indicates the fracture fragment. (Reproduced from Steinmann SP: Coronoid process

MRI typically is not performed acutely and may be helpful to assess elbows with continued
instability.
MRI can be performed to identify ligamentous injuries to the lateral and medial collateral
ligaments.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Most patients with a simple elbow dislocation do not require surgical treatment. Simple
dislocations may be managed via a short period of immobilization followed by movement.
An adult elbow should not be immobilized for more than 2 weeks because stiffness can occur
after short periods of immobilization.
Techniques/Procedures
Typical management at the center of the author of this lesson consists of 7 to 10 days of
immobilization, followed by progressive range of motion.
Serial radiographs should be obtained to confirm fracture healing and maintenance of elbow
reduction.
Outcomes
Most patients with a simple dislocation have excellent clinical outcomes; however, an
extension lag of as much as 30° is not uncommon after an elbow injury, including simple
injuries.
Surgical Management
Indications
Instability and/or recurrent dislocation
Mechanical block to motion

Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction image may be helpful in preoperative planning.
Suture anchors or other means of reattaching the LCL should be available in the operating
room.
The author of the lesson strongly recommends having fixation and replacement options for
the radial head available in the operating room.
Patient Positioning
The most common patient position is the supine position with the arm extended on a hand
table. The author of this lesson uses a large C-arm for radiography, which can be brought in
from the end of the hand table.
An alternative is to place the patient in the lateral position with the arm flexed over a support.
Surgical Approaches
Surgical approaches are dictated by the fracture pattern, and include a posterior approach or
a lateral approach with a separate medial approach if necessary.
The author of this lesson often uses a lateral approach for fixation/replacement of the radial
head and fixation of the LCL.
The two traditional lateral approaches to the elbow are the Kocher and Kaplan approaches.
The Kocher approach involves the use of the interval between the anconeus and the
extensor carpi ulnaris. The Kaplan approach involves the use of the interval between the
extensor digitorum communis and the extensor carpi radialis brevis.
For practical purposes, substantial soft-tissue injury often is present, making the intervals
difficult to assess. The author of this lesson often draws out the radial head and neck and
makes an incision in line with the middle of the radial head.
During both lateral approaches to the elbow, dissection on the radius should not be extended
beyond 5 cm from the joint. This is the location at which the posterior interosseous nerve exits
the supinator to the posterior forearm.6
The radial head can be fixed/replaced via the lateral approach to the elbow, and the LCL can
be repaired, typically directly back to the lateral epicondyle of the distal humerus.
A coronoid fracture can be fixed via a lateral or medial incision. A single lateral approach to the
elbow is associated with the advantage of only one incision; however, risk to the radial nerve in

the brachialis-brachioradialis interval exists. Often, the coronoid can be visualized through the
gap left after the radial head fracture is excised A medial over-the-top approach to the
coronoid also can be utilized. Cubital tunnel release and mobilization of the ulnar nerve are
necessary for this approach; however, the approach is associated with the advantage of
reducing the risk of injury to the radial nerve. The medial approach is ideal for fixation of
anteromedial coronoid fractures and the MCL.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
A systematic approach should be applied to fixation of the elbow. Classically, radial head
replacement or fixation with LCL repair is performed first. If instability persists, fixation of the
coronoid fracture may improve outcomes. Fixation options include screw fixation of the
coronoid, caspsulodesis of the coronoid via a lasso technique of reducing the capsule back
down to the coronoid or via plating, particularly of anteromedial coronoid facet fragments. The
gap left after the radial head is excised may allow for visualization of the coronoid before
replacing the radial head. Classically, if coronoid fixation is required, the coronoid fracture is
fixed first through the space left from the radial head fracture. Coronoid fracture fixation
options include screw fixation of the coronoid, capsulodesis of the coronoid via a lasso
technique of reducing the capsule back down to the coronoid or via plating, particularly of
anteromedial coronoid facet fragments. Next, radial head replacement is performed. Finally,
LCL reconstruction is performed.
A MCL repair may be necessary if the aforementioned steps do not restore elbow stability.
If stability still cannot be attained, a dynamic or static external fixator can be placed. Newer
internal joint stabilizers are another option to restore elbow stability.
Radial head/neck fracture management—The radial column serves as a secondary elbow
stabilizer with an intact MCL and as a primary stabilizer if the MCL is torn. It is a crucial
component of terrible triad injury repair. Therefore, it almost always is repaired or replaced.
Radial head fractures with more than three fragments may benefit from replacement rather
than fixation. If radial head fractures are fixed with the use of a plate, the safe zone should be
used. The safe zone is a 90° arc of non-articulating space on the proximal radius measured
180° to the radial tuberosity to the Lister tubercle.
LCL injuries often are detached from the humeral origin. The author of this lesson prefers to
use suture anchors to repair the LCL. If necessary, an internal brace can be used with suture
anchors at the origin and insertion sites of the LCL to back up repair.

A coronoid fracture can be fixed via suture fixation of the coronoid to the capsule, screws, or
plates. The author of this lesson prefers a suture capsular fixation via a lasso technique for
smaller coronoid fractures.7 The author of this lesson prefers using a pre-contoured medial
plate to stabilize anteromedial facet fragments.8
Postoperative Management
Postoperative management is a balance between the time necessary for soft-tissue and bony
healing and minimizing elbow stiffness associated with elbow immobilization.
The length of time of postoperative immobilization is determined by the strength of the repair.
After a solid repair, the author of this lesson prefers immobilization in a long arm splint for 2
weeks, with passive range of motion of the elbow initiated at 2 weeks postopertively, and
active range of motion initiated at 4 weeks postopertively.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Ensure the necessary equipment is present in the operating room. Even if the radial head is
deemed able to be fixed, an arthroplasty set should be available.
Pre-contoured medial plates for the coronoid are a substantial improvement compared with
prior implant options. An internal brace constructed via suture anchors is a good back up
option for difficult/tenuous ligamentous repair.
Radial head replacement should not be overstuffed. Downsize the diameter of the
replacement by one size. The height of the radial head arthroplasty implant should be in-line
with the lesser sigmoid notch on a lateral radiograph. An overstuffed radial head leads to joint
stiffness9 (Figure 13).
Complications
The most common complication after terrible triad surgery is stiffness.
Another common complication is instability.
Revision surgery is relatively common (20% to 25%).
Other complications include heterotopic bone formation, infection, posttraumatic arthritis,
ulnar neuropathy, nonunion, and malunion.
Nonunion and Infection

9/4/26, 9:47 AM
AAOS | Terrible Triad of Injuries of the Elbow
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004092
21/25

The management of terrible triad injuries may involve difficult, long procedures that require
large exposures. Patients are at risk for postoperative infections. If a nonunion occurs,
consider infection as the underlying problem.
Pain and Stiffness
Pain and stiffness are common after terrible triad injuries. Postoperative pain control often is
aided by physiotherapy, topical anti-inflammatories, and steroid injections.
Partial joint denervation may be helpful for chronic pain after injury.10,11
Instability
Recurrent instability, particularly posterolateral rotatory instability, can occur. This often
results from failure of the LCL complex and can be managed via LCL reconstruction.
Rehabilitation
Postoperative rehabilitation is variable and injury- and surgeon-dependent. Elbows usually are
splinted in 90° of flexion for the first 1 to 2 weeks, after which range of motion exercises are
initiated. If the MCL is intact, the forearm may be splinted in pronation to protect the LCL
repair. If the MCL is injured and the LCL has been repaired, the splint should be applied with
the forearm in neutral rotation.
Passive and active-assisted flexion/extension and supination/pronation are initiated at 1 to 2
weeks postoperatively and continued from postoperative weeks one to six.
Flexion/extension exercises are performed supine in the overhead position in full pronation to
protect the LCL repair.
Terminal elbow extension is limited by 30°, and the limit is progressively decreased to full
extension over the first 6 weeks postoperatively. A hinged elbow brace limiting terminal
extension but allowing flexion and extension may be used.
At 6 weeks postoperatively, the hinged brace is removed, allowing limited lifting and continued
stretching.
Strengthening is initiated at 8 to 12 weeks postoperatively. Unrestricted use is allowed at 4.5 to
6 months postoperatively.
Static progressive stretching is initiated at 10 to 12 weeks postoperatively if concern for
stiffness exists and continued for 8 to 12 weeks before consideration of contracture release.
